claims.text: High-temperature mechanical and thermoelastic behavior in RHEAs is governed by sluggish diffusion arising from their multi-principal-element composition.
The multi-principal-element composition stabilizes a single-phase solid solution.
Suppressed grain-boundary migration enhances creep resistance.
Sluggish diffusion or suppressed grain-boundary migration reduces thermal expansion relative to conventional refractory alloys.
The proposed initial RHEA is a homogenized, equiatomic or near-equiatomic single-phase solid solution, exemplified by MoNbTaW.
High configurational entropy contributes to maintaining the single-phase solid-solution structure.
Atomic mobility is lower in the multi-element matrix because diffusion is sluggish.
Reduced atomic mobility stabilizes the RHEA microstructure at high temperature.
Reduced atomic mobility impedes grain growth.
Under matched high-temperature test conditions, the RHEA will have a lower steady creep strain rate than the conventional refractory-alloy baseline.
Under matched high-temperature test conditions, the RHEA will have a lower coefficient of thermal expansion than the conventional refractory-alloy baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies above 1000°C to single-phase RHEAs but not to multiphase or heavily segregated alloys.
The magnitude of the creep and thermal-expansion effects may depend on elemental selection and processing history.

contradictions.description: The comparator is described as a binary or ternary refractory alloy, but pure Mo is given as an example even though it is elemental rather than binary or ternary.
